title: The fine print of the Belt and Road: what China's loan contracts show, and where the 'debt trap' charge falls short
dek: Secrecy clauses, collateral accounts and creditor-first terms give Beijing real leverage over borrowers, research on its loan contracts shows. But the best-known claims of asset grabs have not held up, and China rejects the charge outright.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
China's Belt and Road Initiative is bigger than ever. Chinese construction contracts and investment in partner countries reached a record $213.5 billion in 2025, according to economist Christoph Nedopil, bringing the total since 2013 to almost $1.4 trillion ([Griffith University](https://news.griffith.edu.au/2026/01/20/chinas-belt-and-road-engagement-hits-record-levels-in-2025/)). The first half of 2026 was another record for total engagement ([University of Queensland](https://news.uq.edu.au/2026-07-review-chinas-belt-and-road-shows-sustained-investment-surge)).

Its critics, including India, say the scheme gives Beijing leverage over poorer countries through secretive and one-sided loans. China says the charge of "debt-trap diplomacy" is a Western invention. The documents now available, including the loan contracts themselves, support parts of both arguments.

## What the contracts say

The most detailed evidence comes from a 2021 study by AidData, the Center for Global Development, the Kiel Institute and the Peterson Institute, which examined 100 Chinese loan contracts with 24 governments and compared them with 142 contracts from other lenders ([How China Lends](https://docs.aiddata.org/ad4/pdfs/How_China_Lends__A_Rare_Look_into_100_Debt_Contracts_with_Foreign_Governments.pdf)). It found:

- **Secrecy:** all post-2014 contracts with Chinese state lenders contained or referred to "far-reaching confidentiality clauses". Only two of the 142 comparison contracts had anything similar.
- **Repaying China first:** close to three-quarters contained what the authors call "No Paris Club" clauses, in which the borrower promises not to include the debt in restructurings with other official creditors.
- **Cash held aside:** 30% of contracts, covering 55% of the money lent, required the borrower to keep a special bank account the lender could draw on.
- **Policy leverage:** more than 90% let the lender cancel the loan and demand immediate repayment after "significant law or policy changes" in the borrowing country. All China Development Bank contracts listed the end of diplomatic relations with China as an event of default.

The authors also set out the limits of their findings. Many terms showed "a difference in degree, not in kind" from other commercial lenders, several "would likely be unenforceable in court in a major financial jurisdiction", and the study did not examine how the contracts were enforced in practice.

## From building to bailing out

AidData's 2023 report, Belt and Road Reboot, found that the scheme had turned from building to rescuing. It estimated that 80% of China's overseas lending in the developing world was supporting countries in financial distress, and that emergency rescue lending rose from 13% of new lending in 2014 to 58% in 2021 ([AidData](https://docs.aiddata.org/reports/belt-and-road-reboot/Belt_and_Road_Reboot_Executive_Summary.pdf)). The share of loans backed by collateral rose from 19% to 72%. The report said Chinese state banks were "paying themselves" by sweeping foreign currency out of borrowers' escrow accounts, and that "these cash seizures are mostly being executed in secret".

A separate study by AidData, the World Bank, Harvard Kennedy School and the Kiel Institute counted $240 billion of Chinese rescue loans to 22 countries by the end of 2021, at an average interest rate of about 5%, against about 2% for IMF rescue loans. Economist Carmen Reinhart, one of its authors, said "Beijing is ultimately trying to rescue its own banks" ([AidData](https://www.aiddata.org/blog/belt-and-road-bailout-lending-reaches-record-levels)).

AidData's latest report, published in November 2025, also found that Chinese lending has become harder to trace, with its measure of how easily the loans can be found falling 62% between 2010 and 2023 ([AidData, Chasing China](https://docs.aiddata.org/reports/chasing-china/Chasing_China_Executive_Summary.pdf)).

## Where the "debt trap" charge falls short

The most-cited example is Sri Lanka's Hambantota port, leased in 2017 to China Merchants Port Holdings for 99 years. A 2020 Chatham House study by Lee Jones and Shahar Hameiri found "there was no debt-for-asset swap": the Chinese company paid $1.12 billion, most of it for an 85% stake in the port's operating company, money which Sri Lanka used to pay other debts and rebuild reserves ([Chatham House](https://www.chathamhouse.org/sites/default/files/2020-08-25-debunking-myth-debt-trap-diplomacy-jones-hameiri.pdf)). Chinese loans were about 9% of Sri Lankan government debt in 2016, and the port project was first pushed by Sri Lankan leaders. Ownership was not transferred and no debt was forgiven, the study found.

The study's wider conclusion was that controversial projects in Sri Lanka and Malaysia were started by the borrowing governments, and that their debt problems came "mainly from the misconduct of local elites and Western-dominated financial markets". Researchers at the Lowy Institute reached a similar finding for the Pacific in 2019, saying China "has not been engaged in deliberate 'debt trap' diplomacy" there, though Tonga owes more than half its external debt to China ([Lowy Institute](https://lowyinstitute.org/publications/ocean-debt-belt-road-debt-diplomacy-pacific)).

Other alarms have not held up. AidData, which published Uganda's Entebbe airport loan contract in 2022, found China Exim Bank "does not have any legal grounds to seize" the airport, though the contract lets the lender take cash from an escrow account ([AidData](https://aiddata.org/blog/aiddata-publishes-a-controversial-200m-chinese-loan-contract-for-ugandas-main-airport)).

China's foreign ministry says the critics have it backwards. Asked about AidData's findings in November 2023, spokesperson Wang Wenbin said that "to describe development resources as a 'debt trap' is to call white black" and that "not a single cooperation partner has accused China of creating 'debt traps'". He said Western lenders and multilateral institutions are the main creditors of developing countries ([China's foreign ministry](https://www.mfa.gov.cn/eng/xw/fyrbt/lxjzh/202405/t20240530_11347630.html)).

## Where leverage has shown

The pressure point is usually not ports, but the slow, private negotiation that follows a default. Zambia, where China was the largest creditor, defaulted in November 2020 and took more than three years to complete a restructuring under the G20's Common Framework. China's positions on how losses should be shared were widely reported as a cause of the delay. In Pakistan, payment arrears to Chinese power producers built under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor have become a recurring strain on public finances, according to Pakistani press reports.

Corruption cases have followed some projects too, from Nepal's Pokhara airport to Ecuador's Coca Codo Sinclair dam ([The Declaration](https://thedeclaration.in/story/china-linked-corruption-cases-kenya-railway-world-bank/)).

## What it means for India

India has refused to endorse the Belt and Road since 2017, because its flagship, the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, runs through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. At the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin in September 2025, India again stayed out of the paragraph in which other members reaffirmed their support.

Several neighbours are now bound more closely to it. Nepal signed a Belt and Road cooperation framework in December 2024, Sri Lanka finished restructuring its debt to China Exim Bank in 2024, and the Maldives agreed debt relief with China in 2025. Bangladesh, where a senior Chinese envoy said this week that work on the Teesta river plan and Mongla port is "advancing steadily", owes China about 9% of its external debt, according to its Economic Relations Division.

For India, the lesson of the contract studies is less about any single port than about secrecy. Confidential loans, collateral accounts and creditor-first clauses make it hard for a neighbour's voters, its other lenders, or India, to know what has been promised and to whom.

## What to watch

- **Bangladesh:** the terms of any Chinese finance for the Teesta project and Mongla port.
- **Pakistan:** talks on arrears owed to Chinese power producers.
- **Belt and Road data:** the next figures on Chinese engagement for 2026, likely in early 2027.
- **AidData and other researchers:** new loan contracts made public, which remain the best test of how the scheme works.
